messages.author: 037b48afaf84ce6e
messages.subject: Multiple likelihood lgcp - tutorial question
parts:
Hello,

I was looking at the lgcp multiple likelihood tutorial on the inlabru website: https://inlabru-org.github.io/inlabru/articles/2d_lgcp_multilikelihood.html#single-likelihood-version.

The components are : 
cmp <- ~ Common(coordinates, model = matern) + Difference(coordinates, model = matern) + Intercept(1)
And the formulas in both likelihoods are:
fml.major <- coordinates ~ Intercept + Common + Difference / 2 fml.minor <- coordinates ~ Intercept + Common - Difference / 2I was simply wondering why we add Difference in both formulas (and why we divide it by 2). How will the Difference spatial field be interpreted in this case? I would've thought that we only add Difference in one of the 2 formulas. 

Also, when we specify both likelihoods, is there a reason that the lik_minor uses the formula for major nests (fml.major) and the major nests data?

Thank you and have a good day,
Edgar Lanoue

messages.author: afb003e064114795
messages.subject: Re: [r-inla] Multiple likelihood lgcp - tutorial question
parts:
Hi,

It’s just a modelling choice. By adding and subtracting half the difference, the model construction doesn’t favour any of the two cases. If we were to add the component to one of the models, and not include it in the other, the model would depend on which of the two we add it to. The add/subtract half option is invariant to the arbitrary labelling. (But for models with more than two cases, such symmetry is much harder to achieve, so then it’s more common to just add more and more to each case.)

For the last question, I think it’s just the names of the likelihood objects that have been swapped; the one that uses the major formula uses the major data, and vice versa, so it’s just the R object names that have been confused.
Finn

Yes, they look like group-specific intercepts.
So either use one fixed effect for each, or a single joint iid random effect (if you fix the precision of that it works even for a small number of groups.
+Int1(1)+Int2(1)
Or
+Int(groupindex)
Finn

Le lundi 22 avril 2024 à 12:37:49 UTC-4, Finn Lindgren a écrit :
The formula expression should match the mathematical model definitions. I don’t think this one matches any of the alternatives in the thread. For example, one would normally only involve a single intercept in each expression. Also, you have to decide if the scaling of each field should be the same in all the models, or if there should be scaling parameters. For that, use the “copy” feature, or make a nonlinear predictor expression with the scaling parameters as latent components. I’m not sure if there’s a full example of that out there…

Le lundi 22 avril 2024 à 11:20:19 UTC-4, Finn Lindgren a écrit :
Hi,

It’s just a modelling choice. By adding and subtracting half the difference, the model construction doesn’t favour any of the two cases. If we were to add the component to one of the models, and not include it in the other, the model would depend on which of the two we add it to. The add/subtract half option is invariant to the arbitrary labelling. (But for models with more than two cases, such symmetry is much harder to achieve, so then it’s more common to just add more and more to each case.)

For the last question, I think it’s just the names of the likelihood objects that have been swapped; the one that uses the major formula uses the major data, and vice versa, so it’s just the R object names that have been confused.
Finn
